idiom_name: no realization - one IO.select loop or a Fiber scheduler, process-per-worker for scale
alternative: a single IO.select (or async-gem Fiber scheduler) reactor dispatching to a Thread/Queue worker pool, plus process-per-worker scale-out (Puma cluster mode/Unicorn) - not a thread pool taking turns in select()
implementation_notes: Ruby exposes every part of the structure - Thread, Mutex/ConditionVariable and IO.select - but its global VM lock serialises Ruby-level execution, so threads that take turns demultiplexing cannot process their handlers in parallel and the pattern's cache-affinity and lock-avoidance arguments do not transfer. What the ecosystem does instead is the workable shape: one thread looping on IO.select and handing connections to a Thread/Queue worker pool (a Half-Sync/Half-Async arrangement), the async gem's Fiber scheduler driving many lightweight tasks over one selector, or forked workers that each own an acceptor. If threads are used at all, size them for blocking calls rather than for parallel event processing.
code_sketch:
queue = Queue.new

def accept_loop(listener, queue)
  loop do
    ready, = IO.select([listener])     # the only thread waiting on handles
    queue << ready.first.accept        # hand off; loop returns to select
  end
end

4.times { Thread.new { loop { work(queue.pop) } } }
pitfalls: Thread#raise and Thread#kill interrupt a thread at an arbitrary point, so a pool protocol built on ConditionVariable can be left mid-transition; do not interrupt pool threads.
A thread that blocks while holding the VM lock stalls every other thread, including the one that should demultiplex; prefer IO.select-driven waiting over blocking calls.
Forked workers that inherit the listening socket must let the kernel arbitrate accepts or use a parent that hands sockets over, otherwise they stampede the same connection.
IO.select and Thread::Queue are the dependable primitives; timer-thread tricks add a thread per timer and destroy the bounded-set assumption the classic design starts from.
